main.title: The Game Awards
main.subtitle: A shared archive of the work we remember
main.summary: A celebration of game makers, with every category winner from 2014 onward.

cards.heading: What the awards celebrate
cards.text: The Game Awards celebrates the people who make games: designers, artists, writers, performers, composers and the teams around them. Created by Geoff Keighley in 2014, the annual show combines awards with performances, announcements and conversations about the medium.

cards.heading: A changing medium, a shared stage
cards.text: An awards archive is also a record of changing priorities. Categories make room for new ways to play and new kinds of work, from independent production and performance to accessibility and community support. Move through the years to read every category winner, then open the official ceremony beside the list.

entries.event_semantics: 2015 anchors the March/April primary interviews, both discussing work before Rapture's release. Dear Esther is an earlier comparison. Planned recordings and intended procedural effects are not asserted as independently audited final-release behaviour.

cards.heading: Keep music, change its players
cards.text: For Dear Esther's commercial release, Jessica Curry kept the music composed for its earlier mod and replaced sampled instrumentation with live players. In a 2015 interview, she described the freedom Dan Pinchbeck had given her to respond to the story. The new recording carried that response into a different performance, preserving the compositions while changing the musicians and materials heard within them.

cards.heading: A recording needs an order
cards.text: Preparing Rapture's recording sessions required a different kind of writing: lists, schedules and decisions about who would play what next. Curry credited orchestrator Jim Fowler's practical knowledge while discussing the planned orchestra, choir and soloists. Cue order considered difficulty, dynamics and the risk of tiring singers. Speaking before the sessions, she described how those arrangements would shape the recording days and guide the people involved. It makes organisation part of the score's production, alongside the more visible work of imagining a melody or hearing a finished performance.

cards.heading: The score becomes the ambience
cards.text: Audio designer Adam Hay offered another view of that same project. He described taking elements of Curry's score into granular synthesis, making sustained textures, recording material onto cassette and bringing it back altered. The process tied ambience to the music instead of laying an unrelated atmosphere beneath it. His account also named a practical constraint: materials built from the soundtrack could share key and tempo. The place the player would hear was being assembled through transformations of composed material, with another maker determining how those transformations behaved.

cards.heading: Other ears enter the work
cards.text: Hay's sound design developed through collaboration. Sony supplied Foley and mixing guidance, while Curry and Pinchbeck discussed ideas with him when he reached a dead end. The team's interest in one another's work provided further opportunities to test a decision. Music, recorded effects and altered textures came together through those exchanges as well as through the tools used to produce them.

main.title: BoxBoy!
main.subtitle: A square makes its own tools
main.summary: BoxBoy! is HAL Laboratory's Nintendo 3DS puzzle platformer about Qbby, a small square who can create connected strings of boxes. Those boxes become bridges, steps, shields or other arrangements for crossing short obstacle courses. The plain monochrome presentation keeps the important relationships visible: the character, the new shape and the space it must occupy. The central ability is deliberately generous in its uses. A small piece of geometry can be detached and moved, or kept attached to Qbby so that the same construction helps his own body reach another place.

cards.heading: A square makes its own tools
cards.text: BoxBoy! is HAL Laboratory's Nintendo 3DS puzzle platformer about Qbby, a small square who can create connected strings of boxes. Those boxes become bridges, steps, shields or other arrangements for crossing short obstacle courses. The plain monochrome presentation keeps the important relationships visible: the character, the new shape and the space it must occupy. The central ability is deliberately generous in its uses. A small piece of geometry can be detached and moved, or kept attached to Qbby so that the same construction helps his own body reach another place.

cards.heading: Think about the shape before placing it
cards.text: Each stage limits how many boxes can be produced in a string. Within that allowance, their arrangement determines what can be crossed or blocked. Qbby can push a detached shape into position, while an attached construction can hook a ledge and help pull him upward. Creating a new string removes the previous one, so an arrangement cannot simply accumulate without consequence. The player has to decide which part of a solution is still needed before replacing it. The restriction makes a compact construction meaningful instead of merely increasing the number of pieces.

cards.heading: Another world asks another question
cards.text: Groups of stages introduce different hazards and mechanical ideas, such as lasers or cranes. The box-making action remains the reference point, allowing each addition to be understood as another question about the same ability. Nearby checkpoints support experimentation when an arrangement fails. BoxBoy!'s visual restraint is useful here: a solution can look almost obvious once its spatial relationship has been recognised. The pleasure comes from turning an ability described in one sentence into a shape that answers the particular obstacle, then discovering that the next world can ask something different.

main.title: Dying Light
main.subtitle: Parkour changes survival in Harran
main.summary: Dying Light combines first-person parkour and survival horror in Harran, where the infected become more dangerous after sunset.

cards.heading: Day and night in Harran
cards.text: Dying Light is Techland?s 2015 survival horror game, launched in North America on January 27. Harran?s rooftops, balconies and ledges offer routes above infected streets. Players search for resources and fight during the day, then face faster, more aggressive predators at night.

cards.heading: Finding routes above the streets
cards.text: Cars, low roofs, balconies and ledges form routes across the city. Players judge which surfaces they can reach and where a run can continue. Learning these paths helps with both exploration and escape.

cards.heading: The danger after sunset
cards.text: After sunset, more dangerous infected change the risks of a familiar route. Exposed streets become harder to cross safely, while rooftops and ultraviolet light offer protection. Planning around the time of day becomes part of travelling through Harran.

cards.heading: Cooperation and continued support
cards.text: Cooperative play lets a group share much of the campaign. Players can distract infected, use elevated positions and take advantage of the surroundings together. Techland continued supporting the game through events, extra content and The Following expansion.

main.title: Life Is Strange
main.subtitle: Max can rewind a decision
main.summary: Life Is Strange follows photography student Max Caulfield, whose ability to rewind time lets her test choices while investigating Arcadia Bay.

cards.heading: Max discovers her ability
cards.text: Life Is Strange is Dontnod?s episodic adventure about Max Caulfield, a photography student who can rewind time. Square Enix released its first episode, Chrysalis, on January 30, 2015. In Arcadia Bay, Max?s conversations, friendships and observations become part of a larger mystery.

cards.heading: Trying another response
cards.text: Max can rewind a few minutes while retaining important information and objects. Players may try a response, watch what happens and choose another. Immediate reactions become visible, but later consequences remain uncertain when a decision is made.

cards.heading: Photographs and details around Arcadia Bay
cards.text: Max?s interest in photography encourages close observation. Posters, messages, bedrooms and school corridors reveal details of the people around her. Optional photographs add small composition challenges alongside the investigation into Rachel Amber?s disappearance.

cards.heading: A story released in five episodes
cards.text: The five episodes arrived over the course of 2015. Choice summaries and percentages let players compare decisions, while gaps between releases encouraged discussion of clues and characters. Writer Christian Divine described combining branching dialogue and gameplay with the culture of the Pacific Northwest.

main.title: The Order: 1886
main.subtitle: A Victorian London between legend and technology
main.summary: The Order: 1886 places Galahad and an order of knights in a reimagined Victorian London.

cards.heading: Knights in an altered London
cards.text: The Order: 1886 places Galahad and an order of knights in a reimagined Victorian London. Ready at Dawn's 2015 PlayStation 4 game combines an old-fashioned city and uniforms with invented weapons and a conflict involving human and supernatural enemies.

cards.heading: Build a believable surface
cards.text: The studio's material research paid close attention to the differences between surfaces such as cloth, leather and metal. These were not simply colours applied to a model: the lighting had to make each material respond convincingly. Close views of coats and weapons make that work unusually visible.

cards.heading: Borrow the camera's imperfections
cards.text: Ready at Dawn also described reproducing characteristics of motion-picture lenses. Focus, framing and optical imperfections contribute to an image intended to resemble something photographed. The result offers a useful distinction when studying game graphics: a technically clean image and a deliberately photographic image are different artistic goals.

main.title: Resident Evil: Revelations 2
main.subtitle: Claire, Moira and Barry return in an episodic island mystery
main.summary: Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is a 2015 episodic survival horror video game developed and published by Capcom  as part of the Resident Evil series.

cards.heading: Claire returns and Barry joins the story
cards.text: Resident Evil: Revelations 2 is Capcom's 2015 episodic survival horror game. Claire Redfield and Moira Burton are abducted and taken to an island, while Barry Burton enters the story with the young Natalia Korda. Each pair combines an armed character with a more vulnerable companion whose abilities help locate objects or threats. Players work together cooperatively or switch between the characters when playing alone.

cards.heading: Two pairs follow the island mystery
cards.text: The story takes place in 2011, between Resident Evil 5 and 6. Claire and Moira disappear during a TerraSave gathering, beginning the first of two connected journeys through the island. Barry later arrives in search of his daughter and meets Natalia, who can sense nearby monsters. Across four episodes, the two pairs approach the same mystery from different points in time. Solving puzzles and negotiating danger requires using the abilities available to both partners.

cards.heading: Platform releases, co-op and critical reception
cards.text: The game was released for PlayStation 3, PlayStation 4, Windows, Xbox 360, Xbox One, PlayStation Vita in 2015 and for Nintendo Switch in 2017 along with the port of the first Revelations. The reviews were mixed to positive and the setting, story, characters and the co-op gameplay were praised, but the graphics and some technical issues were criticized. As of December 31, 2025, the title reached 4 million units sold.
